items.title: Taxation without legislation
paras: Californians were at least asked. This month they voted on Proposition 40, the Billionaire Tax, and on the Associated Press count they rejected it by 52.3 per cent to 47.7 per cent. Stanford’s Hoover Institution reckons 30 per cent of the tax base had already left the state. Whatever one thinks of the outcome, the voters decided.

Australians are never asked. The biggest tax increase of the Albanese years has never been put to parliament, let alone to the people. It is levied by inflation. Milton Friedman called inflation ‘taxation without legislation’. Canberra has turned his warning into a business model.
The trick has two halves. The government first helps create the inflation. It then collects the proceeds through a tax system built to capture every price rise and return none of it.

Start with the first half. Public spending has reached a record 28 per cent of GDP. The non-market sector of health, education and public administration produced 93 per cent of jobs growth in the year to late-2025. Westpac estimates that public spending now underpins 40 per cent of all employment. In February the Reserve Bank governor told a Senate hearing that public spending was adding to inflation. Every extra dollar the government spends competes with private firms for the same workers and materials. Prices rise.

They have risen faster here than anywhere comparable. Consumer prices climbed 4.3 per cent in the year to September. That compares with 3.7 per cent in the United States and New Zealand, 3.5 per cent in Britain and 3.1 per cent in France. The government blames world oil prices. Yet the rest of the world pays the same for oil, and has lower inflation.
Now the second half. Inflation lifts wages, prices, interest and asset values alike, without making anyone richer. The tax system treats it all as gain.

The main collector is bracket creep. Our income tax thresholds are fixed in dollars and never adjusted for prices. A worker whose pay merely keeps up with inflation is pushed into a higher bracket. He pays a larger share of an income that has not grown in real terms. America ended this racket in the 1980s by indexing its federal brackets every year. Malcolm Fraser indexed ours in 1976, then dropped it within a few years once he wanted the revenue without a vote.

The result is a tax rise that no Member of Parliament ever voted for. Since Labor took office in 2022, income tax has risen from 14.3 per cent to 15.9 per cent of household income. On the opposition’s figures, the average earner has lost about $2,000 a year of purchasing power to bracket creep. The Parliamentary Budget Office says the average income tax rate is heading to the highest level ever recorded. Each so-called tax cut hands back a slice of this haul. The Treasurer then takes a bow for generosity with our own money.

The GST does the same work quietly. It is a fixed percentage of prices, so every price rise lifts the take automatically. Fuel excise goes further. It is indexed to inflation twice a year. The only tax our government bothers to index is one that rises for its benefit.

Savers are hit hardest. Interest is taxed in full, including the part that merely compensates for inflation. Take a term deposit paying 4.5 per cent, held by someone on the top marginal rate of 47 per cent. After tax the saver keeps about 2.4 per cent. With inflation at 4.3 per cent, the real value of his savings falls every year. He pays tax on a loss. That is not an income tax. It is a levy on his capital.

Capital gains will soon fare worse. This year’s budget scrapped the 50-per-cent discount from July 2027 and restored the indexation abandoned in 1999. That sounds fair, since only real gains are taxed. But those real gains will be taxed in full at up to 47 per cent, with a new minimum rate of 30 per cent and no averaging. That is among the highest capital gains tax rates in the world. A gain built up over a decade is taxed in a single year, so unindexed brackets push it straight into the top rate. Then there is the government’s own debt. Inflation erodes the real value of every bond Canberra has sold. The holders are repaid in debased dollars. That too is a transfer from citizens to the state that no parliament approved.

This is why the clamour for wealth taxes is so revealing. The Greens want an annual 10-per-cent levy on billionaires. The Australia Institute wants 2 per cent a year on anyone worth more than $5 million. Labor tried to tax unrealised gains on superannuation balances above $3 million and retreated only after an outcry. Yet inflation already imposes a wealth tax on every saver in the country. It just does so without the inconvenience of a vote.

All this extraction comes as living standards fall. Real GDP per head is lower than it was in June 2022. The OECD ranked Australia’s fall in real household income per head in 2024 as the worst of any member country. The public sector grows, the private sector shrinks, and households pay the bill twice. They pay higher mortgage rates as the Reserve Bank fights the inflation. They pay higher taxes as the Treasury pockets it.

Consider the incentives. A government that profits from inflation has little reason to fight it. Every point of inflation raises revenue without a hostile headline or a contested Senate vote. The Treasurer can boast of budget repair built on bracket creep while blaming the Reserve Bank for the pain of higher rates.

The fix is simple to explain. Index the income tax brackets to prices every year, as the Americans do. Tax only real interest, and tax real capital gains at a moderate rate. Require parliament to vote on any rise in the real tax burden, in daylight, where voters can see who voted for it.

Californians were given a ballot and said no. Australians deserve the same courtesy. A tax rise worth having should be worth defending in parliament. One that has to be smuggled in through inflation is not worth having at all.
Peter Swan AO is Emeritus Professor of Finance at the UNSW-Sydney Business School

items.title: What it takes for Australian music to build home-grown audiences
paras: The challenge for Australian composers is not only to write great music, but also finding an audience who will treasure it. ( Supplied: Holly Harrison )
The music written by Australian composers is extensive, varied and unique.
The results of the most recent ABC Classic 100 suggest listeners are often more familiar with composers such as Beethoven, Mozart, Debussy and John Williams than with Australian composers.
The highest-ranked Australian work in the 2026 countdown was Wild Swans by Elena Kats-Chernin, which placed at number 33.
For Catherine Haridy, CEO of the Australian Music Centre, the reason is simple:
Haridy says familiarity with both the music and the people who create it helps audiences form deeper connections.
In the classical music world, this means composers of today are competing with names whose music have been performed and recorded over decades, even centuries.
So the challenge for Australian composers is not only to write great music, but to ensure it is performed, recorded and heard.
Few musicians have witnessed the changing attitudes towards Australian music more closely than Richard Mills.
As a composer, conductor, artistic director and educator, Mills has spent decades helping establish Australian music as a respected part of the nation's cultural identity.
"Growing up in the 50s, there wasn't that sense of obligation to support the culture of creating new music in Australia that there is now," reflects Mills, who is 78.
For Richard Mills, seeing a composer blossom and succeed is one of music's greatest rewards. ( Supplied: Perth Festival/Charlie Kinross )
At most concerts today, you're likely to hear at least one or two works by an Australian composer. Back then, however, Mills says, "Australian music was a rarity."
"I don't think Australian music or Australian composition is any longer the poor cousin to visual art or drama," he says.

Previously, aspiring composers often had to travel to the UK or Europe to study. Figures like Peggy Glanville-Hicks, Miriam Hyde and Malcolm Williamson followed this path, often returning to Australia after their studies, though some remained overseas.

Mills and others of his generation have done much not only to make it possible for composers to study in Australia, but also to have their music performed by organisations like the state symphony orchestras.
But while opportunities have expanded over the past half-century, building a career as a composer still requires persistence, adaptability and resilience in the face of rejection.
Joe Twist belongs to a generation of composers that has benefited from the groundwork laid by leaders like Richard Mills.
Best known as part of the music team behind Bluey, Twist has built a career spanning film, television and contemporary classical music.
Growing up on the Gold Coast, Twist was drawn to the music of Star Wars and Indiana Jones and says he always wanted to "make up my own stuff".
After getting a PhD in composition in Australia, he spent almost a decade applying for scholarships, finally securing an opportunity to study film music in the US.
"It was constant perseverance, because I got rejected many times," he says.
Joe Twist's love of the music in Star Wars and Indiana Jones set him on a path of becoming a film composer.
He went on to work as an orchestrator in Los Angeles, collaborate with Joff Bush on Bluey and contribute to major films before returning to Brisbane in 2020.
Twist says building relationships with colleagues, from film directors to choral conductors, has been crucial to his career.
He believes recordings are essential for helping new music find performers, and from there, an audience.
"People who run music groups often look for music with their ears and not their eyes," he says.
Twist also aims to write music that can be performed by both professional and community groups, creating what he calls "musical gems that are performed over and over".
Growing up and studying in Western Sydney, Harrison says she didn't have the same access to industry networks and major organisations available to students at more established conservatoriums.
Learning the trumpet and drums, however, opened the door to very different musical worlds.
"The trumpet gave me a strict, notated kind of ecosystem, and the drums allowed me to play with anybody anywhere," Harrison says.
Harrison studied composition so she could "capture what I was hearing in my head and share it with other people".
Rather than waiting for opportunities to come to her, Harrison learnt to create them.
"The strength of musicians in Western Sydney is this wonderful amalgam of different people interested in all sorts of different music," she says.
Holly Harrison says we should shout from the rooftops whenever new Australian music gets programmed. ( Supplied )
Instead of writing for conventional ensembles, Harrison often composed for whichever musicians were available.
"You'd have improvisers, rock guitarists, pop vocalists and maybe someone playing the oud," she says.

Alongside opportunities such as the Cybec 21st Century Australian Composers Program, she says she "did a complete blitz of international young composer competitions" to gain experience and build her reputation.
Australian orchestras play a leading role in developing the next generation of composers.
Both Twist and Harrison participated in programs including the Tasmanian Symphony Orchestra's Composer School and the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra's Cybec program.
These initiatives have been credited with enabling composers to reach the next stage of their careers, as well as connecting emerging composers with experienced mentors like Mills.
Similar programs exist across Australia, helping young composers develop their skills, gain practical experience, build industry networks and expand their recording catalogues.

Queensland Symphony Orchestra's Composed program gives secondary school students an opportunity to learn how to write music for an orchestra, while the Australian Music Centre's Momentum Plus program supports composers to record large-scale orchestral works.
Harrison also recommends exploring co-commissioning, where several organisations band together to commission a new work, as a win-win solution.
Harrison's recent Accordion Concerto was premiered by four orchestras around Australia in 2026.
"[It] guarantees the music gets repeat performances [which] can ensure there is life afterward," she says.
Music that is performed multiple times is more likely to become part of the repertoire, according to Harrison.
Catherine Haridy says the repeated success of Beethoven's Symphony No. 9 and Emperor Concerto in the ABC Classic 100 shows how familiarity is built through repeated performances and exposure.

Catherine Haridy is the CEO of the Australian Music Centre, an organisation that helps musicians advocate for their own work and celebrates their achievements. ( Australian Music Centre: New Point of View )
"It appears in films. It's in advertisements. It's at major sporting events. It's in school curricula," she says.
Australian composers deserve equal representation and support alongside the classical music canon people admire and love, Haridy argues.
"Greatness alone does not guarantee discovery, and a work cannot move an audience that has never heard it," she says.
Supporting Australian music requires more than celebrating composers' achievements.
"We have a lot of work and advocacy to do as an ecosystem to support composers and performers through the journey of their careers."

items.title: People with disability call for improved accessibility at music festivals
paras: The ABC's Breanna Medcalfe (centre) gets into the action at the Strummingbird Country Music Festival. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Braedan Jason )
Live music brings people together, but when you live with a disability there are often barriers to overcome.
Mathew Brady, who attended his first music festival as a wheelchair user last month, said it was difficult to take part in such events without extensive planning.
Mathew Brady left hospital for a day to attend his first festival in a wheelchair. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Braedan Jason )
"It's not just a spur of the moment thing, to do something like this," he said.
Rapper Nathan Tessman, known as MC Wheels, lives with spinal muscular atrophy and respiratory distress.
Nathan Tessman has released three hip hop albums. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques )
The seasoned artist and star of ABC TV's Headliners loves sharing his music with live audiences, but it hasn't always been the smoothest ride.
"Music is open for everyone, in some way … the only boundary is getting up on stage and performing it wherever you can," Mr Tessman said.

A 2022 survey by Creative Australia shows that people with disability are under-represented in festival audiences compared to people without disability (40 per cent compared to 45 per cent). They are also less likely to attend arts events (58 per cent compared to 70 per cent).
People with disability cited inaccessible venues and a lack of information about accessibility as barriers to enjoying such events.
MC Wheels makes music in his home studio. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques )
Mr Tessman believes access to — and the availability of — disability toilets are huge barriers to attending gigs for those living with a disability.
He said venues should have people with disability test the facilities before they are labelled accessible.
"I sometimes don't really have any liquids [to drink] at all because I'm trying to make sure that I don't have to go to the bathroom," he said.

Dylan Alcott's Ability Fest, which started in 2018, is Australia's first inclusive and accessible music festival, incorporating a wide range of accessible adaptations to ensure people of all abilities can enjoy live music together.
Ability Fest attracted thousands of music lovers to its inaugural event. ( Alex Drewniak /Ability Fest )
Alcott hopes the accessibility features will allow people with disability to enjoy a festival alongside their able-bodied mates.
Other touring festivals are following suit by implementing accessibility features for festivalgoers with disability.

Country music festival Strummingbird took over the Kawana Sportsgrounds on the Sunshine Coast recently, and festivalgoers with disability were able to take part in the action on their accessible viewing platforms.
Features such as dedicated quiet spaces, accessible toilet blocks, ramps and fast-pass lanes catered for people with different abilities.
It's adjustments like these that give wheelchair users such as Tristan Elder confidence that they can experience live music events without compromising their enjoyment.
Tristan Elder and his mother Carolyn enjoy the view from the accessible deck. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Braedan Jason )
"We went to a music festival in the [Fortitude] Valley a few weeks ago and there just wasn't anything there for Tristan," his mother Carolyn Elder said on his behalf.
She said the experience at Strummingbird was "really special" because Tristan could see the main stage from the accessible viewing platform.
For people with vision impairment or blindness, seeing the stage can be the least of their challenges, according to Simran Handa, a researcher at Griffith University.
Simran Handa believes music is a universal language for everyone to enjoy. ( Supplied: Simran Handa )
"The concert experience does not begin when the performer walks in those doors. It begins when someone searches that event," she said.
Simran Handa's grandmother inspired her to improve the experiences of people with vision impairments. ( Supplied: Simran Handa )
Inspired by her grandmother Shreemati Rani Bhola and mother Ranju Handa, who both have vision impairments, Dr Handa believes music is a universal language everyone should be able to enjoy.
She is now interviewing music venues and events with in a bid to bridge the gap between venue intentions and the real-world experiences of visually impaired people.

items.title: Hundreds waiting for their own records from Tasmania's education department
paras: Tasmania's education department has a backlog of hundreds of applications for personal information. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke )
Hundreds of people are waiting to receive their own personal records from Tasmania's education department.
The department holds foster care and youth detention records, which are important for victim-survivors of child sexual abuse applying for redress or preparing a civil court claim.
The department says it is working to reduce the backlog and hopes to have it down to 300 outstanding applications by the end of the year.
Hundreds of people are waiting for access to their own records from Tasmania's education department, a department secretary has told the state's ombudsman.

In a letter from assistant department secretary Ross Smith to Deputy Ombudsman Natasha Freeman, Mr Smith said the department had 483 outstanding applications, some more than two years old, made under both Right to Information (RTI) and Personal Information Protection legislation.
The letter, dated June 19 this year, was released to the ABC under RTI provisions.

"Of the 483 outstanding applications, a significant proportion of applications (approximately 98 per cent) relate to individuals seeking access to their own historical records, e.g., former wards of the State, who the Department expects are seeking access to their records for the purposes of applying to the National Redress Scheme or to commence a civil claim against the State," Mr Smith wrote.
The Department for Education, Children and Young People holds foster care records, youth detention records and other education-related records.
In his letter, Mr Smith said the other 2 per cent of outstanding applications were "requesting information concerning the operations of the Department".
"Of the 483 applications, approximately 66 per cent are requests from law firms or support agencies, with 34 per cent made by individuals.
"The oldest outstanding applications are from April 2024, and the Department expects to have these finalised by the end of 2026."
Personal records from the department are an important source of information for lawyers preparing civil claims on behalf of victim-survivors of child sexual abuse. ( ABC News )
For victim-survivors of child sexual abuse who are taking civil legal action, their personal records are an important source of information for the lawyers preparing their claims.

The records can help establish when and where a child in foster care was placed; they can help identify foster carers and workers who may be relevant to the claim and, in some cases, document any disclosures of abuse.
Angela Sdrinis Legal (ASL) is one of the firms that specialises in historical child sexual abuse cases.
Applications by its lawyers on behalf of victim-survivors account for about 100 of the outstanding applications.

"It's very distressing for our clients in particular because institutional abuse victims have already navigated a pretty traumatic experience with an institution and then they feel like they're battling another one," principal solicitor at ASL in Hobart, Annabelle Ward, said.
Annabelle Ward says RTI delays cause further distress for her clients. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden )
Law firm Maurice Blackburn has at least 50 outstanding RTI applications made on behalf of its clients in Tasmania.
"It's incredibly frustrating for people, particularly where the state is the defendant in the case.
"Our clients are asking if the state is deliberately not handing over the documents to prevent them from making a claim."
Mr Rule said, "survivors shouldn't have to wait months, sometimes years, for their own records".
John Rule says the delays are "incredibly frustrating". ( ABC News: Danielle Bonica )

Child sexual abuse victim-survivor Sam Morgan, who alleges she was sexually abused in the 80s while in foster care and at a Tasmanian government school, waited 23 months for her personal records to be released by the department under RTI.
"When it drags on for two years … the anxiety just becomes horrific," she told the ABC last month.
In 2018, Tasmania abolished the time limits on bringing a civil claim for historical child sexual or serious physical abuse.
That, along with the introduction of the National Redress Scheme, has led to a significant increase in requests for personal information from the department.
Tasmania's Department for Education, Children and Young People holds foster care and youth detention records, as well as school records. ( ABC News: Coco Veldkamp )
In his letter to the deputy ombudsman, Mr Smith said the department was working with applicants to refine their applications for personal information "to improve timeliness".
He said four permanent and four fixed-term positions had been added to the department's RTI team.

"If all positions can be filled and onboarding finalised by July [2026], the Department expects to reduce the backlog to 300 outstanding applications (from 483) by the end of December this year," Mr Smith wrote.
Ms Ward said the policy change to enable the "refining" of RTI applications was welcome.

"We're really grateful to the Right to Information team for coming up with this policy because, if it works, it will minimise a lot of the delays; it allows for a lot more flexibility and a lot more nuance."

items.title: Directions under Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 – Nagar Sahakari Bank Ltd., Etawah
paras: The Reserve Bank of India issued Directions under Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 to Nagar Sahakari Bank Ltd., Etawah, vide Directive No. LKO.DOS.SED.No.S29/12-03-000/2026-2027 dated May 15, 2026, for a period of six months up to close of business on November 18, 2026. The Reserve Bank of India is satisfied that in the public interest, it is necessary to further extend the period of operation of the Directive beyond close of business on November 18, 2026. 2. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank of India, in the exercise of the powers vested in it under sub-section (1) of Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, hereby extends the Directive for a further period of three months from close of business on November 18, 2026, to close of business on February 18, 2027, subject to review. 3. The aforesaid extension and/or modification by the Reserve Bank of India should not per se be construed to imply that the Reserve Bank of India is satisfied with the financial position of the bank. 4. All other terms and conditions of the Directive under reference, shall remain unchanged. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1510

items.title: ED arrests six persons in cross-border drugs smuggling network
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): The Enforcement Directorate ( ED ) has arrested six persons in connection with an investigation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) case linked to a cross-border drug smuggling network, the agency said on Tuesday. ED 's Delhi unit arrested these accused in different operations launched on October 11, October 18 and October 20. The arrested accused are identified as Lovejit Singh alias Labba, Manjeet Singh alias Manna, Prabhjit Singh, Gurjot Singh, Ramandeep Singh, and Gurpreet Singh. "A major drug trafficking operation involving smuggling of heroin from Afghanistan into India was unearthed during investigation," said the ED in a statement. The PMLA investigation was initiated on the basis of seizure of 293.81 kg of heroin from containers imported by Sandhu Exports at Nhava Sheva Port by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence and seizure of 352.71 kg of heroin from two vehicles and a flat in Faridabad, Haryana, by the Delhi Police Special Cell. Thus, a total of 646.52 kg of heroin has been seized so far. ED investigation revealed that the arrested persons, Lovejit Singh, Manjeet Singh, Ramandeep Singh, Gurjot Singh, Gurpreet Singh and Prabhjit Singh, coordinated the smuggling, storage and distribution of heroin across Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi.

"These individuals were key members of a syndicate that smuggled heroin from Afghanistan and Iran, concealing them within shipments of talc stone and gypsum powder," said the ED . Accused persons incorporated Sandhu Exports, a front company owned by Prabhjit Singh, to carry out the smuggling of drugs, informed the federal agency. ED uncovered the highly sophisticated heroin smuggling and money laundering network where identification of multiple bank accounts, cash transactions, and operational expenses by the accused has been made. "Accused disguised the origin of the illicit funds, which were further layered and integrated into seemingly legitimate financial activities. It was also revealed that the syndicate did not make any payments to Afghan suppliers until the drugs were sold in local markets." Further, the agency said the accused used cash payments to purchase multiple vehicles including Toyota Fortuner, Etios and Hyundai Verna etc in second hand market for trafficking from the storage Hubs to further distribution. The ED investigation revealed that cash was used for the purchase of high-end smartphones and encrypted communication apps were used to coordinate smuggling activities. "Drugs smuggled from Iran and Afghanistan used to be imported via the Nava Sheva port in Mumbai, later stored at a rented godown in Shivpuri, Madhya Pradesh and further distributed for local supply in parts of Delhi, Punjab and Haryana. Transportation was carried out in lesser quantities of 10 kg to prevent detection by law enforcement agencies. Earlier, a property in Jandoli Village (Rajpura, Punjab), multiple bank accounts in the names of accused persons, and fixed deposits have been attached by ED ," added the agency. (ANI)

Previously, a property in Jandoli Village (Rajpura, Punjab), multiple bank accounts in the names of accused persons, and fixed deposits were attached by the ED . (ANI)

items.title: Indian students in Kazan delighted as PM Modi arrives for BRICS Summit
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Kazan [ Russia ], October 22 (ANI): Indian students in Kazan , Russia , are happy and excited about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's arrival at Hotel Korston , as he attends the 16th BRICS Summit . Notably, PM Narendra Modi on Tuesday touched down in Kazan city of Russia to participate in the 16th BRICS Summit and received a warm welcome. He is here to attend the 16th BRICS Summit , being held under the Chairmanship of Russia . To welcome PM Modi , students from India studying in Russia also sang a welcome song as they awaited PM Modi 's arrival at Hotel Korston . An Indian student from Pune, Saniya said that the students are quite excited to greet PM Modi . "Maybe we will get the opportunity (to meet PM Modi ) as many students are here (at Hotel Korston )... We are very excited. We are lucky to have this opportunity and we are happy to see him," she told ANI. An Indian student from Bihar, Shaurya Pratap said, "We are very happy to welcome PM Modi and we have prepared a song for him and we hope he likes it." Surbhi from Delhi said, "I have been here in Kazan since 2019 and today, we are going to sing a song for PM Modi and we are very excited about that." Parul, a final-year medical student, who has been in Kazan for the last five years told ANI, "We are really grateful that we got this opportunity to welcome our dear Prime Minister." Arti Pawar from Maharashtra said, "I have been living here for the past three years. I am very happy that PM Modi is coming here." Mrunmayi from Nagpur, Maharashtra said, "All the students here are quite enthusiastic as PM is going to come soon. We are too much delighted to welcome him." Meanwhile, ISKCON volunteers - from the Russia n and Indian communities were seen chanting 'Hare Krishna, Hare Ram' ahead of PM Modi 's arrival. While speaking with ANI, Sergoy, an ISKCON volunteer, said, "'Hare Krishna is a Mahamantra. This visit of PM Modi to Kazan , Russia is an important one for us. We are happy." Another ISKCON volunteer said, "We want to welcome PM Modi here in Kazan . It's a great honour for us to welcome him here We are very excited to see him." A Russia n citizen, Alexander said that the people there will welcome PM Modi by singing a song and that he is happy with PM Modi 's visit to Kazan . He said, "We have made a banner and we will also sing a song to welcome PM Modi ... I returned from India just two days back and directly came from Delhi to Kazan to see PM Modi . I am very happy that he is coming to Russia ." Notably, ahead of his departure to Russia , PM Modi shared a post on X and wrote, "Leaving for Kazan , Russia , to take part in the BRICS Summit . India attaches immense importance to BRICS, and I look forward to extensive discussions on a wide range of subjects. I also look forward to meeting various leaders there." The Prime Minister's office in a statement quoted PM Modi as saying, "I am departing today on a two-day visit to Kazan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the Russia n Federation, to attend the 16th BRICS Summit ." "India values the close cooperation within BRICS which has emerged as an important platform for dialogue and discussion on issues concerning the global developmental agenda, reformed multilateralism, climate change, economic cooperation, building resilient supply chains, promoting cultural and people to people connect, among others," PM Modi said. The statement further said that the expansion of BRICS with the addition of new members last year has added to its inclusivity and agenda for the global good. "Building upon the Annual Summit held in July 2024 in Moscow, my visit to Kazan will further reinforce the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia . I look forward to meeting other leaders from BRICS as well," the PMO statement said. The 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan is being held under the chairmanship of Russia from October 22-24. During his visit, PM Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from BRICS member countries and invited leaders in Kazan . The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "The Summit, themed 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security,' will provide an important platform for leaders to discuss key global issues." It further said, "The Summit will offer a valuable opportunity to assess the progress of initiatives launched by BRICS and to identify potential areas for future collaboration." This visit marks, PM Modi 's second visit to Russia this year. He travelled to Moscow in July to attend the 22nd India- Russia Annual Summit where he held a bilateral meeting with President Putin. He was also conferred with Russia 's highest civilian award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle at the Kremlin in Moscow. BRIC, as a formal grouping, started after the meeting of the Leaders of Russia , India and China in St Petersburg on the margins of G8 Outreach Summit in 2006. The grouping was formalized during the first meeting of BRIC Foreign Ministers on the margins of UNGA in New York in 2006. The first BRIC Summit was held in Russia 's Yekaterinburg in 2009. It was agreed to expand BRIC into BRICS with the inclusion of South Africa at the BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting in New York in 2010. South Africa attended the 3rd BRICS Summit in Sanya in 2011. A further expansion of BRICS took place in 2024 with five new members - Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. (ANI)

items.title: "Singapore plays key role in Act-East policy": Rajnath Singh at India-Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Dr. Ng Eng Hen , Singapore 's Minister of Defence , has begun his three-day visit to India . As part of his visit, Dr. Hen co-chaired the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi, with his India n counterpart Rajnath Singh . The Summit began on Tuesday morning, with India n Defence Minister Rajnath Singh welcoming the Singapore delegation warmly. He noted that the strategic partnership the two countries share is a "testimony of increasing closeness between our countries." Singh said, " The meeting is happening at a time when India marks the decade of India 's Act in Policy, in which Singapore has played a key role in promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and developed strategic connectivity with country institutions." Building upon Singh's remarks, Dr. Ng Eng Hen said, "You reminded us that this is the 10th year since your Act East Policy. From Singapore 's perspective, India has always been part of the East. Whether you choose to act or look, we consider you part of the area." He said that while remembering the history of Singapore , India has been an important partner. " When we started the Singapore armed forces, one of the countries that we asked early on to see whether they could help us was India ." Hen highlighted that such historical memoirs serve as important reminders and "reflects how we feel that India is very part of our area. We are delighted that our ten years of bilateral relations have been very much improved in defence and all-round strategic partnership." Hen also thanked PM Modi for visiting Singapore earlier this year and noted that the visit was an excellent meeting. A day before, the Ministry of Defence had announced the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi on October 22, 2024. The release noted that between India and Singapore , "The engagements have diversified to include wide-ranging contacts between the Services, military-to-military exchanges, high-level visits, capacity building and training programs, cooperation in UN Peacekeeping, ship visits and bilateral exercises." Inaugurated in 2016, the India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue is a key platform to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation between Singapore and India . The fifth edition of the Defence Ministers' Dialogue took place in January 2021 through virtual teleconference. During the meeting, the two parties showed confidence in the outcomes of the meeting that would result in providing impetus to the entire spectrum of the bilateral engagement as well as to the regional security architecture. (ANI)

items.title: "India matters most for future of planet" says British High Commissioner Lindy Cameron
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): In recent times when climate change has become a pressing issue with countries across the world being ravaged due to climate catastrophes, it becomes imperative to discuss and deliberate upon global actions that can help the world rise up and meet these challenges. At the NDTV World Summit's a discussion was held on the theme, "India Matters The Most For Future Of Planet". Participants in the discussion included Erik Solheim, Former Minister of Climate and the Environment of Norway; Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India; Shishir Priyadarshi, President Chintan Research Foundation; Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative. "India is the country that matters the most for the future of the planet and climate change. India's ambition for development should not in any way be constrained by the responsibilities of the planet," Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India, emphasised. She noted that the UK is committed towards the Multilateral Development Banks (MDB) reforms, technology and research support in India to aid the efforts. "Every dollar invested in resilient infrastructure pays 4 times over," said Cameron. "Lived experience of climate emergencies helps people to understand why their government needs to take policy action now," she added. Further talking about the need for urgent government action, Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative said, "Series of disasters affecting both developed and developing countries are serving as a wake-up call. As rich countries will get more and more affected by climate change which they did not imagine till a couple of years ago, most vulnerable countries are going to be struggling with impacts who also have very less capacity to deal with it. India is taking a leadership role in the global fight against climate change. Initiatives such as Global Biofuels Alliance, International Solar Alliance, and Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure are some efforts taken by India in recent years to manage the climate crisis. (ANI)

items.title: Mukka Proteins Limited Announces Rs 98 Crore Preferential Issue for Acquisition and Expansion
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel VMPL Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: Mukka Proteins Limited , India's largest fish meal and insect meal producer and a leader in the animal protein industry , has announced the approval of a preferential issue worth Rs 98 crore by its Board of Directors. This strategic move will help Mukka Proteins in its ongoing domestic and international acquisition and expansion efforts, reinforcing its position in the global market. A significant portion of the funding will come from the promoter and promoter group, underlining their commitment to the company's robust growth strategy. The preferential issue will comprise up to 1.96 crore equity shares at Rs50 per share, aggregating to Rs98 crore. This price includes a premium of Rs49 per share on the face value of Rs1. Mukka Proteins will use the raised capital to enhance production capabilities and meet the growing global demand for sustainable and high-quality protein solutions, particularly in the fishmeal and insect meal sectors. In a clear show of confidence, Mukka Proteins' promoters have committed to a capital infusion of INR 60 crore through a preferential allotment of equity shares. This significant financial backing will be used to strengthen the company's financial position, reduce debt, and fund key operational improvements. Mukka Proteins has consistently embraced sustainability, having commercialized insect protein as a significant innovation for the aquaculture and animal feed industry. The company's waste-to-food initiatives have contributed to environmental sustainability, particularly in collaboration with the Mangaluru municipality for waste management. These efforts not only align with global environmental best practices but also enhance circular economy processes, focusing on converting municipal waste into valuable protein and oil products. Mukka Proteins is known for its strong commitment to ecological preservation, evident through the development of sustainable products such as fishmeal, fish oil, and insect protein. As a key player in the aquaculture and nutraceutical markets, Mukka contributes 25-30% of the market share in India's fishmeal and fish oil industry. The company plans to expand its operations further, capitalizing on this capital infusion to enter new markets and enhance its global footprint.

This issuance is subject to necessary statutory and regulatory approvals, including shareholder approval at the upcoming Extra-Ordinary General Meeting (EGM) on November 16, 2024. Managing Director and CEO Harris commented, "This preferential issue is a major milestone for Mukka Proteins as we continue to strengthen our market position. Our growth plans remain firmly rooted in sustainability, and this capital will enable us to scale up production, diversify our product offerings, and reinforce our commitment to responsible and eco-friendly business practices." Mukka Proteins Limited is poised to capture new opportunities in the animal protein sector, reinforcing its legacy of innovation, sustainability, and operational excellence. Mukka Proteins Limited : Mukka Proteins Limited is a leading manufacturer and exporter of fish meal , fish oil, and other protein products. The company has built a reputation for delivering high-quality, sustainable protein products to a global customer base. With a commitment to innovation and quality, Mukka Proteins serves industries including aquaculture, pet food, and agriculture across multiple continents. Headquartered in Mangalore, India, Mukka Proteins operates state-of-the-art processing facilities that meet stringent international standards. The company is dedicated to sustainable practices and has been at the forefront of environmental stewardship within the protein processing industry. (ADVERTORIAL DISCLAIMER: The above press release has been provided by VMPL . ANI will not be responsible in any way for the content of the same)

items.title: India to grow at 6.8 pc in FY25 and 6.6 pc in FY26: S&P Global Market Intelligence
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): India's growth, although moderating, remains strong with a forecasted average of 6.8 per cent for the fiscal year 2024-25 and 6.6 per cent for 2025-26, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence . Despite a slowdown in economic momentum due to weaker public-sector investment, the outlook for India's economy is buoyed by several positive factors. Easing inflation, favourable monsoon conditions, and increased government social spending are expected to boost household demand. Additionally, healthy corporate balance sheets are playing a vital role in supporting the recovery of private investment. S&P Global Market Intelligence has released its October Global Economic Forecast update, emphasizing a steady global economic expansion supported by policy stimulus, while acknowledging risks from geopolitical factors. The outlook highlights moderating inflation and easing monetary policies as key factors steering the global economy towards a "soft landing."

Ken Wattret, global economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence , remarked, "The global economy is on track for a soft landing, with inflation rates moderating and monetary policy easing becoming more widespread. Still, geopolitical developments have the capacity to dampen or even derail the expansion." Report forecasts an annual real GDP growth rate of 4.3 per cent in 2024 and 4.4 per cent in 2025 for the region excluding China and Japan. Aiding this growth is resilient domestic demand, as regional central banks adopt more accommodative monetary stances. The start of the US Federal Reserve's easing cycle in September is creating more room for interest rate cuts, prompting several central banks, including those in the Philippines, New Zealand, Hong Kong SAR, and Indonesia, to lower rates. S&P Global Market Intelligence underscores that while the global economic outlook remains positive, risks persist. Geopolitical tensions could potentially derail economic progress, especially in regions with heightened uncertainties. Nonetheless, policy measures aimed at stimulating growth, coupled with moderating inflation, are setting the stage for a sustained economic expansion. (ANI)

items.title: The "shameful" measles data that lost the US its elimination status
paras: Bleak The “shameful” measles data that lost the US its elimination status Measles became endemic in the US months ago—and it’s only accelerating

1 ... ... ... A child with measles. Credit: Greene, Charles Lyman A child with measles. Credit: Greene, Charles Lyman Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav International health authorities formally announced on Tuesday that the US has lost its measles elimination status, a hard-fought public health triumph won in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. The loss had been widely expected by public health experts for months, and the decision was leaked by the press last week. Still, having the designation officially stripped stings.

After the announcement Tuesday, public health experts, doctors, and political leaders decried the dramatic backslide for the US, calling it “ shameful ” and a “ national embarrassment .” News articles point to the staggering vertical rise of measles cases this year, currently over 5,400 cases , more than any other year since 1991. An explosive measles outbreak in Pennsylvania accounts for over 1,500 of those cases . There have been 10 confirmed deaths across three states, several deaths just in the last week.

But the measles data that caused the US to lose its status—the bits of it that are public at least—paint a darker picture of where the US is in its rematch with measles, the most contagious virus known on Earth. For one thing, almost none of the data from this year—the cases, the explosive Pennsylvania outbreak, the deaths—factored in to the loss. It was lost earlier. What’s happening now is a runaway epidemic.

The US measles elimination status is a designation granted by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is a regional division of the World Health Organization. Last week a committee of experts assembled by the PAHO, called the RVC, met to review measles data for countries across the region, including the US. (RVC is short for the Measles, Rubella and Congenital Rubella Syndrome Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission.)

For their review of the US data, the RVC heard from an independent committee of experts from the US, called the NSC, which presented measles data collected from January 2025 onward. (The NSC is short for the US National Sustainability Committee for the Elimination of Measles, Rubella, and Congenital Rubella Syndrome.)

According to the PAHO, an elimination status is lost when epidemiological and laboratory data shows that a single viral lineage has spread continuously for at least 12 months within a country. At this point, the virus is considered to be reestablished or endemic. So, to withdraw the US elimination status, the RVC needed to see evidence that a single introduction of a measles virus led to a 12-month-long chain of cases, which requires a lot of data.

The full set of data the NSC presented to the RVC is private for now. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention needs to review and approve such data for public release, which can be a lengthy process that has not yet occurred.
The Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC, did not respond to a question from Ars Technica regarding when the data may be released.

But Ars Technica spoke with the chair of the NSC, Noel Brewer, who tried to talk through the pieces of data in the NSC report to the PAHO that he could discuss—these are pieces that have already been made public at some point by others, such as by state health officials or researchers. Brewer said the NSC presented the PAHO with genetic data spanning January 2025 to January 2026, and also epidemiological data that extended to June 2026.

In a press briefing Tuesday, officials for the PAHO made clear that only some of the data presented by NSC factored into its assessment of the US elimination status. The RVC only looked at the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, which doesn’t include the massive outbreak ongoing in Pennsylvania, which began in April. “The number of cases in Pennsylvania did not actually contribute to the decision that was made by the Reverification Commission,” Rhonda Sealey-Thomas, PAHO’s assistant director, explicitly told reporters Tuesday. For 2025, the US reported 2,289 cases nationally.
Still, there was no ambiguity about the US losing its status; “multiple lines of data show clearly that the US has sustained transmission of measles,” Brewer told Ars.

Brewer, who is also the Gillings Distinguished Professor in Public Health at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, confirmed that the beginning of the end of US elimination was January 20, 2025, in Texas —that date was included in the letter PAHO sent to the US informing it of the loss of elimination status. That Texas outbreak was declared over on August 18, 2025, after 762 cases were confirmed in the state. But the virus carried on elsewhere and is still simmering.

“Since January 20, 2025, the US, Canada, and Mexico have been passing measles cases back and forth across borders,” Brewer said, and the national data shows multiple, “genetically distinct” measles introductions into the US. “However, there is one genomic lineage that predominates across the cases and ties many of them, the majority of them, together,” he said.

For people closely tracking the US measles status, a key question has been whether the big outbreaks that followed the initial one in Texas were clearly linked. If they were, it would be immediately obvious that the US had lost the elimination status; but if not, and the outbreaks were driven by different virus introductions, the US could have kept its measles-free status based on the technicality of how the status is defined.

Data that might hold the answer to this question has been elusive. The measles strain in Texas, D8-9171, appeared similar to the viruses seen subsequently in big outbreaks in Arizona and Utah . But, the strain was also similar to those from Mexico and Canada. Generally, there can be relatively small genetic changes among measles viruses, and genetic data alone is not used by PAHO to evaluate elimination. In June of this year, ProPublica tried to get at the answer itself, conducting its own genetic analysis of measles strains in the US. It concluded that “the measles virus still spreading in Utah as of this May is very closely related to the one that sickened Texans over a year ago.” But the outlet acknowledged this wasn’t a “smoking gun.”

To date, the question lingers. Brewer cannot yet explicitly disclose what the NSC reported to the PAHO about possible links between the Texas outbreak and any of the subsequent large outbreaks in 2025. That includes the one in nearby Utah or one in South Carolina, which began in October 2025 and ultimately tallied 997 cases by the time it was declared over in April, 2026.
For its part, the PAHO did not respond to multiple requests for comment from Ars Technica on linkages between the outbreaks.

But, in a twist, Brewer noted that the answer to the question might be moot; the lineage that started in Texas on January 20 might not be the only one that has been sustained and could have lost the country its status. There are “one or two that have gone on for more than 12 months,” he said.

With the designation now formally lost, health and medical experts are coming to grips with the reality that measles is once again endemic in the US. Details of how the US should move forward are up for debate; the US is now required to submit a “corrective action plan” to the PAHO, outlining how the country intends to regain its elimination status. But, the fundamental solution is obvious and straightforward: The US needs to increase vaccination rates.

While the virus has been raging in religious communities with low vaccination rates, the entire US has seen slipping vaccination coverage. That makes it easier for the virus to gain a foothold virtually anywhere.

A protective vaccination rate is considered to be 95 percent; according to the latest data , only 92.4 percent of kindergartners were vaccinated with the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year. Only 10 states have MMR vaccination rates at or above the 95 percent threshold. Meanwhile, non-medical exemptions from school vaccination requirements have never been higher, at 4 percent. Currently, 24 states have exemption rates at or above 5 percent, meaning that even if they are able to vaccinate every single non-exempt child, they would still not meet the 95 percent target. And this is just the data for young children. The vaccination coverage for adults is another concern, and the data there is scarce. In Pennsylvania’s massive outbreak, 1,055 of the 1,561 cases this year have been in adults ages 18 and older (less than 1 percent of the cases were fully vaccinated).
While some health officials have noted optimistically that 92.4 percent in children is just a few percentage points from the target, the reality of bringing up vaccination rates is more onerous.

PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa stressed the point in the press briefing Tuesday: It’s “not the national average or the average in the state or even the average in a big city, you need to guarantee that in every community, village, you have this vaccination coverage up to 95 percent. This is very important,” Barbosa said.

The point has been demonstrated in the US. In 2019, the US came very close to losing its measles elimination status . Unlike now—when the virus is on a nationwide rampage, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases—in 2019, the US nearly lost its status from a single, large outbreak that spread in New York. Though it didn’t explode on a national level, it took 11 months to stamp out in those under-vaccinated communities. In that year, the US reported 1,274 measles cases total.

The situation in the US has only gotten worse, and the outlook is bleak, Brewer warns. “The measles outbreaks in Canada and Mexico are winding down,” he noted. “However, in the US, our measles problem continues to accelerate. There is no end in sight.”

items.title: Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories
paras: Still waiting on Spore 2 Will Wright’s next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories With MyMems , Wright says he wants to “turn the simulation inward.”

13 ... ... ... Your personalized memories may differ from this idyllic MyMems concept art. Credit: Gallium Your personalized memories may differ from this idyllic MyMems concept art. Credit: Gallium Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav The computer gaming world hasn’t heard much from Will Wright ( SimCity , The Sims ) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright’s subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA . Now, well over 15 years later, Wright is starting to promote his next digital simulation, which will use generative AI technology to craft a game-like experience from players’ memories.

MyMems , which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright’s previous projects by “turn[ing] the simulation inward,” as Wright’s Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning . The game will mine memories provided by the player to create digital people that can then form teams to solve puzzles in the game world.

“If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?” Wright says by way of example in the release. “If I had to build a bridge across a short chasm, which three people from my life would I choose to help me?”

In an accompanying announcement video , Wright talks about how the “plausible behavior” in a game like The Sims still didn’t effectively capture the nuances of people he encounters in real life. “It was nowhere near them understanding my claustrophobia or why my sister and I fought so much… We’re actually taking parts of your life, your memories, your experiences, people you know, and turning that into a game that’s very personal.”

Wright said MyMems will be able to extract generalized themes from your memories into self-contained areas that Wright compared to the various parts in a theme park: Sports, vacations, injuries, memories, and deaths could all be the basis for their own zones to play in. Players will also have the option to create worlds based on shared memories with family, friends, and co-workers, for example.

Since this is 2026, it shouldn’t be surprising that MyMems is making heavy use of generative AI (with a “proprietary behavior engine” on top) to transform your typed-up memories into simulated locales and characters. In the announcement video, Wright praises the “entirely open-ended” AI systems Gallium is using “to extract from the stories and whatnot based upon the memories you put into the game.”

But Wright’s focus on mining memories for simulation content predates the current generative AI boom. What has now become MyMems started off as Proxi , a mobile simulation that was first announced in 2018 as “a game of self-discovery, a game where we actually uncover the hidden you.” But after years of pre-production work (as outlined in an excellent Vulture piece earlier this year ), Wright’s Gallium Studios finally ran out of funding in late 2024, leading to mass layoffs for the small team and an uncertain future for the project.

Now the idea has been revived thanks in large part to a partnership with AI middleware firm Artificial Agency . Until now, that company has mainly been focused on agentic systems that can create “virtual players” to playtest a game or serve as a partner for human players.

Now, Artificial Agency’s marketing says the company’s AI tool will be used to create “a personal behavior model and a knowledge graph” from players’ memories, drawing some unsettling comparisons to big tech surveillance.
“Meta knows what you click,” the company writes. “Netflix knows what you watch. Nobody knows what you remember. MemDNA learns from your memories locally and only with your permission.”

Wright said the partnership with Artificial Agency will let Gallium benefit from “off-the-shelf” AI solutions without having to “become an AI research company” in its own right. He also said the collaboration will help limit costs by providing a cheaper option than the “really expensive” frontier models that might be overkill for a project like this.
“Right now AI has opened a vast new design area and I’m enjoying, you know, exploring that as a designer,” Wright said.

items.title: The real reasons we keep seeing big tech outages – it isn’t just hackers
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print A Microsoft office in New York Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images In the past week, a Microsoft outage locked millions of people out of their email accounts , computer problems at a US bank stopped payments and a glitch in air traffic control systems grounded flights in the US. Even the US National Security Agency (NSA) reported that its secure intranet NSANet had fallen over , and Apple’s online services also went offline . The cluster of failures prompted rumours of a coordinated cyberattack by a foreign state or a hacking spree powered by AI.

Speculation about such ideas was so rife that the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, was forced to reassure people that the government had “zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind”.

But why are we seeing so many outages all at once? There are certainly hackers, including state-backed ones who stage coordinated attacks. For instance, a boss at the UK’s intelligence, security and cyber agency – Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ) – recently told New Scientist that Russia and China are staging “relentless” cyberattacks against the UK using AI. AI has also allowed even non-experts to uncover dramatic bugs in widely used software . But that isn’t what we have seen in recent days.

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) put its air traffic control outage down to “routine maintenance” in which copper communications lines were being upgraded to fibre-optic cable . The head of the FAA, Bryan Bedford, echoed Rubio in a press conference and said: “We see zero evidence of anything nefarious.”

Bank outages were put down to a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase. Microsoft blamed a trifecta of problems for its email issues: an old software bug, malfunctioning internal data connections and server capacity. As for the NSA glitch, the spy agency said only that problems arose “during scheduled routine maintenance”, and didn’t respond to a request for comment. Apple pinned its issues on an internal update .

The flurry of outages, then, is partly down to coincidence and partly explained by a chronic lack of investment in resilient infrastructure, says Daniel Dresner at the University of Manchester, UK. He says that not only is there no indication that these outages are linked, but there is no evidence that they are malicious hacks.
“Things are failing all the time,” says Dresner. “This stuff is really fragile.”

Dresner says there has been an increasing trend – exacerbated by new AI models that can create computer code with unprecedented speed – to prioritise new features and updated interfaces over data validation and reliability.

“We all have what a colleague of mine called the ‘Big Mac mentality’: we want it with all the trimmings and we want it with speed. We’re happy because it’s working – until it fails,” says Dresner. “We wanted agility and we ended up with fragility.”

These sorts of failures aren’t rare, says Alon Hillel-Tuch at New York University. “The honest answer is that it isn’t really all happening now. Outages like these happen all the time. What’s unusual this week is that several big ones landed close together just as everyone started looking for a pattern. As for why it all seems to be happening at once, large outages are far more common than people realise,” he says.

Tim Stevens at King’s College London says that the technology sector has been developing profitable and desirable tools, but failing to build and maintain the infrastructure on which those tools rely . He says it is like a car firm selling sports cars when the roads are littered with potholes and dead ends. Spending money on fixing or improving infrastructure brings no immediate profit, so is overlooked.
Global race to update computers as AI discovers most disruptive hack yet

“This is what we built and this is what we have predicted for years and years and years. It’s coming home to roost,” says Stevens. “If you’re going to build an entire global system on demonstrably insecure networks and systems, then this is what you’re going to get. I don’t think there’s anything more than coincidence in the current set of events, it’s just they seem to have come in a short period of time.”

George Loukas at the University of Greenwich, UK, says that US government cuts to cybersecurity efforts like the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency will certainly have worsened matters overall, but that the real reason for the enormous disruption we see when services go offline is that we all tend to use a very small number of digital tools.

“We are depending increasingly on digital environments which tend to be an oligopoly. Five years ago, that wouldn’t be the case. We would have exactly the same event, but not the same impact,” says Loukas.
The growth of domestic solar installations opens the possibility of hackers targeting their smart inverter devices as a way to cause widespread power-system failures

In many industries, says Loukas, governments have stepped in and broken up monopolies, but he has seen less progress in the digital world. Until there are many thriving, competing rivals in every sector of technology, we will be vulnerable to enormous outages that bring everything grinding to a halt until staff at one company can find a fix.

Stevens says that AI has led to the discovery of a great number of software bugs, which have required lots of patches. That low-hanging fruit has now been picked and we are seeing a slowdown, he says, but that burst of activity is likely to have been a good thing overall for security.

However, there are huge hurdles between us and a more resilient online world, due to the “perverse economics of cybersecurity”, says Stevens. “If you’re going to test something to oblivion [to make sure it’s secure and resilient], then your competitors have already stolen the market. It is what it is, and I’m quite pessimistic about how to address this. It’s an uphill battle, particularly when the economic incentives point in the opposite direction.”

items.title: How Great Britain’s two representatives at the ATP Finals are performing ahead of their final group-stage matches
paras: Great Britain hit a new low on the in the men’s singles discipline this year. For the first time since 1995, no British man won a singles title on the ATP Tour .
The likes of Jack Draper, Cameron Norrie and Arthur Fery were all unable to do so. However, in the doubles discipline, Britain possesses some of the Tour’s finest players.

Two of those players – Henry Patten and Neil Skupski – are taking part in the year-ending ATP Finals in Turin, Italy. Patten, who recently called out ATP Chairman Andrea Gaudenzi following his no-show at the year-end world number one ceremony, is partnered with fellow world number one, Harri Heliovaara. items.title: Steve Johnson thinks he knows the real reason Taylor Fritz chose to play the Stockholm Open, ‘I’m sure…’
paras: Taylor Fritz won the Stockholm Open after failing to qualify for the ATP Finals. With a place in the year-end finals up for grabs, Fritz failed to convert match point against Carlos Alcaraz at the Paris Masters, before losing in three sets, 7-6, 5-7, 3-6.

Many expected the American to end his season after such a heartbreaking defeat, but he chose to travel to Sweden instead. Bouncing back, Fritz won the Stockholm Open , defeating Argentina’s Thiago Agustin Tirante, 6-2, 4-6, 7-6, in the final.

But why did Fritz play the ATP 250 event when ATP Finals qualification was off the table? His fellow American, Steve Johnson, thinks he knows why. “There is nothing more on-brand than Taylor Fritz going to play a 250, completely irrelevant for 99% of people who follow tennis and watch tennis.
items.impact: The American is expected to return to tennis ahead of next year’s Australian Open, which begins on January 17.

items.title: ATP Finals Day 5 Predictions Including Ben Shelton vs Rafael Jodar
paras: All four men could technically advance, though it would take something stunning for Rafael Jodar to reach the semifinals. Meanwhile, Alexander Zverev has already clinched his semifinal spot after two strong wins to open the group stage, but he still has more ranking points to play for in his final match.

So, who do you think will win and book their semifinal places ? Fils has played solid tennis in both of his ATP Finals matches so far, coming close in a loss to Shelton in one match while wearing down Jodar in the other.

Zverev, though, has appeared on another level this week. His serves are crisp and untouchable, and his baseline play has been some of his best in years. Fils doesn’t have much that can really outhit him.

items.title: How Ben Shelton and Arthur Fils can qualify for the ATP Finals semi-finals ahead of their final group matches
paras: Alexander Zverev has become the first man to qualify for the semi-finals of the ATP Finals. Zverev secured his spot in the last four after defeating Ben Shelton 6-2, 7-6 on Tuesday, extending his head-to-head record over the American to 7-0.

Shelton and Frenchman Arthur Fils are now the most likely players to finish second in the John McEnroe group. Rafael Jodar, who is yet to win a match at the Finals, can also still qualify for the last four.

With a 1-1 record, Shelton currently finds himself second in the John McEnroe group – leading Arthur Fils in the standings due to their head-to-head record at the event this year [1-0]. How do you think Ben Shelton will perform next season after hiring Juan Carlos Ferrero? If Shelton defeats Rafael Jodar and Zverev defeats Fils, Shelton will finish second in the group and qualify for the last four.

Friendships are built by repeated contact, not by being liked
items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
items.do: Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800.
